findings: Account 7200, inventory shrink adjustment, went from $8,900 to $71,200, a $62,300 increase at 700 percent, is marked over threshold, and not one sentence in the memo mentions it. A sevenfold jump in shrink is theft, spoilage or a physical count correction, and each of those has a different answer. I want the count sheets, the depots the loss sits in, and whether this is one count or an estimate spread across four.

Account 6400, bad debt expense, fell $52,500 or 84.7 percent, is marked over threshold, and gets no commentary at all. A drop that size is either the non-recurrence of a one-off reserve or a release back through income, and those read very differently. If any part of it is a release I need to know which receivable was let go and what changed about its collectability inside one month.

Account 5100, inbound freight, fell $43,500 or 15.1 percent, is marked over threshold, and has no sentence of its own. The one freight explanation in the memo, the renegotiated rates effective July 1, is spent on account 5000 instead. The driver and the account it belongs to are both in this file and the memo has connected them to the wrong things.

S3 attaches the driver to the wrong account. Inbound freight is account 5100 and the header keeps it separate from cost of product sold, so renegotiated freight rates cannot drive the $147,000 decline in account 5000. What actually drove account 5000 is volume, since product revenue fell 3.8 percent and product cost fell 3.4 percent, which is the ordinary relationship and not a purchasing win.

S4 has the direction backwards on account 6100, fleet fuel. The table runs $91,200 to $108,700, an increase of $17,500 or 19.2 percent, and the sentence says it declined $17,500. The driver fails with it, because diesel coming off its June peak would push the line down and the line went up almost 20 percent in a month when revenue fell.

S5 describes an unrecorded liability and then calls it policy. The fuel was burned in July so roughly $9,800 belongs in July, and it should be accrued rather than left to land in August. The consequence is not cosmetic. Corrected, account 6100 is $118,500 against $91,200, an increase of $27,300 at 29.9 percent, which clears both the $25,000 and the 10 percent test. Fleet fuel should be a starred line carrying commentary and it is not, so the omission has changed which accounts the memo is required to explain.

Saying in S5 that deferring the last week of fuel is consistent with normal practice makes it a systematic cutoff failure rather than a one-off. If every month excludes a week of fuel then the liability is permanently understated on the balance sheet, and the size of the tail changes with diesel prices, so the error is not self-correcting. That practice needs to stop at this close, not be documented in a variance memo.

S6 misstates the amount on account 6000, warehouse wages. $781,900 less $702,500 is $79,400, and the sentence says $74,900. The digits are transposed and $4,500 goes missing. The table percent of 11.3 percent is computed off $79,400, so the prose and the schedule disagree on the largest expense line in the company.

The driver in S6 contradicts the rest of the table. Overtime for a summer volume peak cannot sit beside product revenue down $214,000 at 3.8 percent and cost of product sold down $147,000 at 3.4 percent. Volume fell in July. Warehouse wages rising 11.3 percent into falling volume is the finding, and it points at headcount, a rate change or an accrual true-up rather than a peak that did not happen.

S7 and S8 contradict each other on account 6200, repairs and maintenance. S7 says the depot repair program closed in June with no further repair spend expected this year, and S8 says the $36,400 in July is the second phase of the dock program at Southline. A program cannot be closed and in its second phase at the same time. If phase two ran in July then phase three is a commitment nobody has disclosed.

S9 puts account 6600 in the wrong period. Marketing of $96,400 that relates to a regional trade show in September is a cost of a September event, so it belongs in prepaid expenses until the show happens, not in July operating expense. Up to $96,400 of July cost is sitting a month or two early. The sentence is also circular, since explaining why July is elevated by saying July is elevated against a quiet June is not a driver.

S10 misstates the amount on account 7100, interest expense. $76,300 less $74,900 is $1,400, and the sentence says $1,900, which is the 1.9 percent column rewritten with a dollar sign. $1,900 appears nowhere in the table. The driver is also thin, because a genuinely higher average revolver balance would move interest more than 1.9 percent, and I would want the daily balances before accepting that sentence.

S11 is arithmetically false. Operating expense as the memo defines it, accounts 6000 through 7200, is $702,500 plus $91,200 plus $118,600 plus $62,000 plus $22,000 plus $74,900 plus $8,900, which is $1,080,100 in June, and $781,900 plus $108,700 plus $36,400 plus $9,500 plus $96,400 plus $76,300 plus $71,200, which is $1,180,400 in July. Total revenue is $6,774,000 in June and $6,622,500 in July. That gives 15.9 percent and 17.8 percent, not 15 percent in both months, and the ratio worsened by about 188 basis points.

The conclusion in S11 is also the opposite of what happened. Operating expense rose $100,300, or 9.3 percent, while total revenue fell $151,500, or 2.2 percent. The cost base did not move with volume, it moved against volume, and that divergence is the single most important sentence this memo could have contained. It is instead reported as stability.

The margin definition parks a product loss outside product cost. Account 7200 holds $71,200 of inventory that no longer exists, yet gross margin is defined as account 4000 less account 5000 only, so shrink never touches it. Put the loss where the product went and July cost is $4,202,200, giving a margin of 22.2 percent against June at 23.6 percent on the same basis. The reported margin of 23.5 percent flatters the month by roughly 130 basis points.

S1 rests on evidence that is not in the file. The claim that the 3.8 percent decline in account 4000 is consistent with the same month last year cannot be tested against a table holding two months, and no prior year figure appears anywhere. A school nutrition slowdown also sits oddly on a June to July comparison, since school accounts wind down as the year ends rather than a month after. Give me the prior July or take the sentence out.

The threshold rule lets the largest dollar movements through untouched again. Account 4000 moved $214,000 at 3.8 percent, account 5000 moved $147,000 at 3.4 percent and account 4100 moved $55,000 at 5.3 percent, so $416,000 of movement clears the $25,000 test, fails the percent test and requires no comment, while account 6400 at $52,500 is starred because a small base makes its percent large. The rule is selecting for volatility rather than for size.
